proposal: The Mandate recommends that EPA restore the position that a new pollutant from an already regulated source category cannot be regulated without predicate findings, automatically withdraw proposed rules not finalized within the statutory one-year period, and revise the general section 111(d) regulations so existing-source programs are source-specific and deferential to states. For hazardous air pollutants it recommends that unregulated emission points of an already regulated pollutant not require MACT standards, that section 112 rules be harmonized with section 111 rules for the same sources, and that cost-benefit analysis focus on the targeted pollutant with co-benefits identified separately. It does not name specific power plant rules for repeal.

status_summary: EPA has repealed or proposed to repeal specific Biden-era rules rather than revising the general Clean Air Act provisions the Mandate describes: the repeal of the 2024 Mercury and Air Toxics Standards amendments (91 FR 9088, published 2026-02-24) took effect 2026-04-27, and D.C. Circuit challenges to it were placed in abeyance on 2026-08-13. On 2026-09-17 EPA published a final partial repeal of the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards (91 FR 58954, effective 2026-11-16) and a supplemental proposal (91 FR 59002, comments due 2026-11-02) to rescind the 2015 power plant findings and repeal all remaining power plant greenhouse gas standards; the final rule did not act on the June 2025 proposed finding that these emissions do not contribute significantly. EPA's 2026-04-22 proposal on the oil and gas hazardous air pollutant standards (91 FR 21672) takes the primary position that it need not add standards for previously unregulated emission points, which resembles one Mandate recommendation, and a law firm article reports that the MATS repeal analysis did not monetize co-benefits from pollutants outside the rule's target, which parallels another. No rulemaking revising the general section 111(d) regulations, adding automatic withdrawal of unfinalized proposals or harmonizing sections 111 and 112 was found; separately, an EPA interim final rule of 2025-07-31 (90 FR 35966) extended compliance deadlines in the 2024 oil and gas new source standards, including moving the Super Emitter Program start to 2027-01-22.

timeline.event: EPA publishes two proposals: repeal of all greenhouse gas standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants (with a proposed finding that these emissions do not contribute significantly to dangerous air pollution, and a narrower alternative), and repeal of the 2024 MATS amendments.

EPA publishes an interim final rule (90 FR 35966, effective on publication) extending compliance deadlines in the 2024 oil and gas new source standards (control devices, covers and closed vent systems, leak repair, process controllers, storage vessels), extending the state plan deadline for existing sources, and moving implementation of the Super Emitter Program to 2027-01-22; a related final rule on the extensions followed on 2025-12-03.
EPA announces the final repeal of the 2024 MATS amendments, leaving the 2012 requirements in place.

EPA's final repeal of three 2024 MATS amendments (stricter filterable particulate matter limit and compliance demonstration for existing coal units, stricter mercury limit for lignite units) is published (91 FR 9088), effective 2026-04-27; EPA estimates present-value savings of $670 million at a 3 percent discount rate over 2028 to 2037.

EPA proposes its technology review of the oil and natural gas production hazardous air pollutant standards (91 FR 21672): primary position is that section 112(d)(6) does not require it to add standards for previously unregulated emission points now, with an alternative proposal to set standards for them; comments were due 2026-06-22.

A law firm article describes the MATS repeal's regulatory impact analysis as declining to monetize health benefits from pollutants outside the rule's statutory target (particulate matter co-benefits), a shift it says may affect later rulemakings.

The D.C. Circuit places the consolidated MATS repeal cases (Air Alliance Houston v. EPA, No. 26-1070, filed 2026-03-30; State of Illinois v. EPA, No. 26-1072, filed 2026-03-31) in abeyance while EPA considers a petition for reconsideration filed 2026-04-24 (per Harvard's tracker).

timeline.event: EPA publishes the final partial repeal of the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards (91 FR 58954; repeals the existing steam unit emission guidelines, carbon capture standards for modified coal units and phase 2 standards for new base load turbines; effective 2026-11-16) and a supplemental proposal (91 FR 59002) to rescind the 2015 power plant findings and repeal all remaining power plant greenhouse gas standards; comments on the supplemental proposal are due 2026-11-02. The final rule states EPA is not acting on the June 2025 proposed no-significant-contribution determinations at this time.
Environmental groups file a D.C. Circuit petition against the partial repeal the same day (American Lung Association v. EPA, No. 26-1238), per a law firm summary.

title: Revise Clean Air Act section 111 and 112 rules toward source-specific regulation
uncertainties: Federal Register pages were read through summarizing fetches; the web rendition of 91 FR 58954 ends before the amendatory instructions, so a change to the general 111(d) regulations in the regulatory text cannot be fully excluded, though none is mentioned in the preamble. The MATS litigation details come from Harvard's tracker, which itself shows a year typo for the petition dates; the American Lung Association petition (No. 26-1238) comes from a law firm summary and was not checked against the court docket. Federal Register queries for general section 111(d) implementing regulations returned only state plan approvals; the Unified Agenda entries on reginfo.gov were not read, so a planned general 111(d) rulemaking cannot be excluded. Not checked: the Good Neighbor Plan, whether the oil and gas hazardous air pollutant review was finalized, and any EPA action on harmonizing sections 111 and 112. Progress is a judgment call: it was lowered from 50 to 35 because only one of the six recommendations on page 427 (no new standards for unregulated emission points) has a matching proposal, and the power plant actions the record rests on are parallel rather than direct matches. EPA announced on 2026-10-07 that it would propose to rescind the oil and gas Super Emitter Program; no proposal had appeared in the Federal Register by 2026-10-13, so it is not listed as an event. The 2025-12-03 final rule that followed the 2025-07-31 interim rule was seen only as a related-document listing.
